paras.en: Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.

Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.

Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.

But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.

Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.

Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.

Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”

Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.

But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

articles.title: Go Minimal—the Ridge Wallet is 20 Percent Off Right Now
articles.author: Les Shu

paras.en: Everyday carry (EDC) enthusiasts and social media influencers have made the Ridge Wallet a favorite for its durability and minimalist design. But it’s not just hype. In her testing, WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe gave it high marks, saying, “I can’t see myself using anything else,” even though she’s not a minimalist and didn’t fall for the “ridiculous” marketing. It’s also one of the wallets I use on vacation, when I just need to carry a few credit cards without drawing attention to the usual George Costanza bulge in my pocket.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Select Ridge Wallet styles are currently on sale for $76 (normally $95) as part of the brand's Friends & Family sale, which also has discounts on other Ridge accessories like pocket knives, power banks, luggage, trackers, and more. If the wallet turns out to not be your thing, Ridge will refund you as part of its 99-day risk-free trial.

As Strampe mentioned in her review, the Ridge Wallet will look unfamiliar to newbies. In fact, it may not feel user-friendly at first. The wallet acts like a sandwich for all your cards, using two aluminum pieces held together with screws and elastic bands. It holds up to 12 cards, but you can adjust the opening with the T-5 Torx screws and included screwdriver to fit exactly how many cards you need.

If you’re a minimalist, the Ridge Wallet can help you stay that way. For Strampe, she can’t imagine the Ridge replacing her purse—she still needs to carry her car keys and other necessities. But it does help her keep all her cards—credit, driver’s license, Costco—in one place without rummaging through her bag or using a bulkier wallet.

The Ridge Wallet is somewhat customizable. You can add a cash strap or clip on the outside; there’s even a money clip with a slot for an AirTag. There’s also a chain and D-ring attachment, and you can personalize your Ridge Wallet with colored screws.

articles.title: A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
articles.author: Vittoria Elliott

paras.en: Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk third-party website.

The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.

“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”

“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that had been what could be characterized as an incident.

The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.

“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.”

Accenture currently has more than $3.5 billion in contracts with the federal government, nearly $605 million of which are with the DOD. The company also contracts with other federal agencies, such as the Department of Education, the General Services Administration, and the Department of Energy, among others. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Triner also notes that the increasing pressure on contractors to deliver projects faster and at a lower price point is at odds with prioritizing safety and security. “Unfortunately, everyone is operating in a system where there are competing rules and incentives, and that existed before AI, but now it’s the same problem on speed,” says Triner.

The coding environment accessed by the Accenture contractor is run on the Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet), a DOD network used for unclassified information. While it does connect to the internet—contractors and employees can access their emails and web browsers through the network—it is heavily secured.

According to the source, in order to automate the process of writing code and spinning up cloud servers, the contractor gave their login credentials to the Claude agent. This gave the agent administrative access and allowed it to bypass the security controls enforced through the normal login process. The AI agent—which was not only writing code but also committing it or saving the code into the system on behalf of the Accenture employee—needed to connect out to the internet to perform its tasks. In doing so, it appears to have sent the contractor’s login credentials, passwords, and a map of NIPRNet out to a third party website.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: WIRED is declining to name the third party website so as to protect the system from further vulnerability, but National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has previously identified it as high risk because it has a vulnerability that could let hackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials.

The system the AI agent accessed contained CUI. “Information from a CUI environment is not supposed to leave that infrastructure,” says the source. “There is no insight about what happened to the information, including the login credentials, after it was sent to [that service], whether it’s been retained”

Depending on the agency and its work, CUI can include anything from personally identifiable information (PII) to proprietary business or contracting information. According to the DOD’s website, CUI can include information on “the securing and safeguarding of explosives, hazardous chemicals, or pipelines,” documentation related to the designs of “military or space equipment or technology;” and “the exact location and quantities of radioactive material.”

Distinct from the actual data, a map of it could be incredibly valuable to a hacker. “Once an attacker understands how those things fit together, even if those things are public information, what is sensitive is how we are putting those things together and turning that into actionable intelligence,” says Triner.
While a map might not get a hacker into a system, he says, it could help an adversary move faster once they do have access and “help an attacker understand where the crown jewels are.”

Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker and faculty at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy, says that an AI agent running code in NIPRNet presents a “huge problem, and there are huge national security impacts.”

Williams notes that while individual pieces of data or information might be considered CUI, “when that unclassified information is aggregated, that can become classified itself.” For instance, the location of certain hazardous materials might be CUI, as might be information about the vulnerability of the facilities that house them. Combined, however, they could reveal information that would be kept classified.

But this is not the only way classified information may have been put at risk. Frequently, tools and code are tested in NIPRNet before being deployed into more sensitive systems like the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), the military’s secured network for classified information, and Joint Worldwide Intelligence Communications System (JWICS), a secure intranet for top secret information. Both SIPRNet and JWICS are air gapped, a security measure that means they are not connected to any outside networks. On a practical level, that means SIPRNet and JWICS would be extremely difficult for a hacker to access remotely.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But with the login credentials exfiltrated by an AI agent, a hacker could access NIPRNet and insert a backdoor or other malicious code into a tool or system. Without proper review, this code could end up deployed in one of the air gapped systems.

“The code could operate completely normally in NIPR and do something malicious and undisclosed in a SIPR network, that is 100 percent possible,” says Williams. Exfiltrating data out of these networks would be difficult, he adds, but malicious code could be used to attack the systems from the inside. “I think the most likely thing would be some kind of distributed denial of service attack,” he says.
Triner says that even something more subtle, such as slowing down intelligence operations and activities, could cause damage and make users lose trust in a tool, even once the problem is fixed.

As vibe coding, or prompting an AI assistant to write the code for a product described by an engineer, is becoming more common, vetting code is becoming more of a challenge. AI is capable of generating code at a volume that far surpasses human productivity, making it time consuming and difficult to vet.

“When you’re using an agent, you have no idea of the supply chain or even the inference chain of what has ultimately generated the code,” says Williams. “A lot of the code that these LLMs were trained on is itself vulnerable, and they can regurgitate the same kinds of architecture, and architectural issues that we see in other code.”

The government does have a way to identify flawed code in NIPRNet. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) scans code for bugs and flaws before allowing it to run. But Williams notes that a hacker-inserted “backdoor is not a vulnerability, even if we may not want it there,” and therefore would likely fly under the radar of SAST’s detection. SAST also does not usually identify structural issues in the logic chain of how code is created.

There’s no indication that hackers were able to get into a classified or top secret system. Still, Williams says, the incident should raise significant alarms. “Architecturally, any information about NIPR that you can’t see through open source intelligence, DOD considers a close hold regardless of whether something touches a classified network,” he says.

This is not the first time the DOD has been made vulnerable because of AI-related issues. Last year, ProPublica revealed that Microsoft was using “digital escorts” on its projects with the federal government, wherein American employees with security clearances would be overseeing code written by outsourced workers in China. Experts who spoke to ProPublica said that the program presented a particular security risk because the American employees were often not able to vet the code themselves, leaving openings for malicious code to be inserted unknowingly into government systems.

articles.title: N.C. lottery player wins $1.9M from her first-ever online game

paras.en: Oct. 29 (UPI) -- A North Carolina woman won a $1,939,727 jackpot from the very first online lottery game she ever tried to play, officials said.
Mount Pleasant resident Donna Gray told North Carolina Education Lottery officials she came into Digital Instant games as a complete novice on Aug. 1.
"I've bought scratch-offs over the years but this was the first time trying this," she said.
Gray selected the PowerMax Cash game, and on her very first $1 play, she won the $1,939,727 jackpot.
"It started rolling and just kept rolling," she recalled. "I thought it would be like $100 or something."
The winner said she rushed to tell her husband.
"I said, 'I won big,' but he didn't believe me," Gray said. "It took us both a couple days to believe it."
Gray said her winnings will go into savings.

articles.title: Look: 'Bosch: Start of Watch' photos introduce 'Bosch' prequel series

paras.en: Oct. 29 (UPI) -- MGM+ is introducing the new series Bosch: Start of Watch.
The streaming service shared first-look photos for the show Thursday featuring Cameron Monaghan and Omari Hardwick.
Bosch: Start of Watch is a prequel series to Bosch, the Prime Video series starring Titus Welliver as LAPD detective Harry Bosch, which had a seven-season run from 2014 to 2021.

Start of Watch explores the origin story of Bosch, a character who first debuted in the Michael Connelly novels. Monaghan plays a young Bosch, a rookie cop, while Hardwick stars as veteran officer Eli Bridges.
Set in 1992 Los Angeles, the series "will explore a city on the edge, teeming with racial tension, gang violence, and a fractured LAPD."

"Amid routine calls and growing unrest, Bosch finds himself drawn into a high-profile heist and a web of criminal corruption that will test his loyalty to the badge and shape his future as the detective who lives by the code, 'Everybody counts or nobody counts,'" an official synopsis reads.

Other cast members include Ariana Guerra, JD Pardo, Kathleen Wilhoite, William Fichtner, Rafi Gavron, Raphael Sbarge, Azita Ghanizada, Kenneth Miller, Seamus Dever, Ryan McPartlin, Marco Rodriguez and Shelli Boone.
Bosch: Start of Watch will have a two-episode premiere Jan. 10, 2027, on MGM+.

articles.title: Watch: Portable phone charger explosion caught on camera

paras.en: Oct. 29 (UPI) -- Firefighters in California are warning about the dangers of lithium ion batteries after a portable phone charger's explosion was caught on camera.
The Vacaville Fire Department reposted a video on Facebook showing what happened inside Vacaville resident Keri Lynne's home.
The video shows a woman sitting on a sofa inside her living room when a portable phone charger suddenly explodes and bursts into flame next to her.
The woman was not injured and the residents were able to extinguish the flames before they spread to the rest of the home.
The department said the incident highlights the dangers of lithium ion batteries, and offered advice including purchasing only from reputable manufacturers.

"Be cautious of inexpensive, off-brand chargers and power banks sold through online retailers, including Amazon. Look for products with recognized safety certifications, such as UL or ETL," the post said.

Officials also recommended owners of lithium battery-powered devices keep them off of combustible surfaces, always use the proper charging cord and watch for warning signs like battery swelling and excessive heat.

articles.title: Universal Music Q3 Earnings: Subscription Streaming, Downtown Integration Pay Off
articles.author: Elizabeth Dilts Marshall

paras.en: Universal Music Group (UMG) said on Thursday (Oct. 29) that accelerated subscription streaming revenue, margin improvement and the integration of Downtown Music Group helped drive revenue growth of 11.7% revenue growth in the third quarter.

Revenue of €3.39 billion ($3.87 billion), which grew by 5.3% excluding the Downtown acquisition, benefited from 1.81 billion euros in subscription streaming revenue, which rose 17.9% from a year ago. Downtown and its suite of independent businesses contributed 9.5% of that increase in subscription streaming revenue, according to a press release.
“Downtown is the most important acquisition UMG has made since EMI,” UMG CEO Lucian Grainge said on a call discussing the results. “The numbers are already proving why we made this deal.”

Adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization rose 9.0% in constant currency or 7% when stripping out the impact of Downtown, to 729 million euros ($831.06 million). Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded by 0.4 percentage points to 21.5%, compared to 22% a year ago, as strength from the recorded music business competed with lower profitability in music publishing and merchandise.
The music company’s third-quarter revenue came in ahead of consensus analyst estimates, which had projected revenue of approximately €3.37 billion, according to MarketWatch

Top sellers in the quarter included Mrs. Green Apple, Olivia Rodrigo, Stray Kids, Ariana Grande and The Beatles. Physical growth was broad-based across North America, Japan and Europe and across both front line and catalog.

Recorded music revenue overall rose by 14.7% in constant currency to 2.56 billion euros ($2.92 billion), boosted by a 19.2% increase in subscription revenue driven by wholesale price increases. Ad-supported streaming revenue grew by 13.5% and physical sales rose by 17.4%. Recorded Music adjusted EBITDA margin excluding Downtown improved to 26.2%, helped by lower A&R spending and tighter cost controls.

Music publishing revenue grew 7.5% in constant currency, or just 1.5% excluding the Downtown acquisition. Digital publishing revenue rose by 11.8%, but adjusted EBITDA fell 3.5% on a difficult comparison to last year’s quarter.
Merchandise revenue fell by 4.6% on fewer major tours than the third quarter 2025, although strong sales directly to consumers, like through UMG’s storefronts, helped offset this weakness.

UMG recently rolled out another raft of layoffs related to a cost-cutting plan first announced in 2024 that the company says will deliver 250 million euros ($271 million) in annual savings by the end of 2026.
UMG’s stock price was 0.6% higher at 15.84 ($18.06) as of 1:35 p.m. in New York.

“Overall, we’re encouraged by the progress we saw in several areas this quarter, including the acceleration in subscription revenue, continued strength in physical sales, and improved profitability,” UMG CFO Matt Ellis said on the earnings call. “At the same time, we recognize that there is more work ahead of us. That work is underway.”

articles.title: Watch Ice-T Bust a Ghostly Tale on Halloween ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Episode
articles.author: Anna Chan

paras.en: What’s spookier than ghosts and goblins? Try the heinous crimes that the squad of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit deals with every week. But for the Thursday (Oct. 29) episode of the long-running NBC crime procedural, the show dips its toes into the supernatural, and Billboard has a first look at one of the scenes.

While gathered in the squad room, Sgt. Odafin Tutuola (rapper-actor Ice-T) kicks off the haunting chatter, and Det. Amanda Rollins (played by Kelli Giddish) reveals how she once went to a palm reader who predicted — accurately — that she would one day have three children. When Capt. Curry (Aimé Donna Kelly) calls it a “lucky guess,” Rollins concedes it’s a possibility, “but there are some things out there without an explanation.”

Newish SVU detective Griffin (Corey Cott) sides with criminal profiler Rollins, recalling a ghostly encounter from his youth. “It was a Saturday morning. I was the only one awake in my house. I look at the end of the hall, there’s a beautiful woman there. Don’t smile!” he shoots back when his fellow officers scoff. “A beautiful woman, and she waved at me — and then she was gone.”

Ever the skeptic, Tutuola suggests Griffin’s dad was perhaps “stepping out” before making clear his stance on the unexplained phenomena. “I mean all I’m saying is there’s no ghosts, there’s no poltergeists,” he declares emphatically. But then, the sergeant — who should probably display an “I Want to Believe” poster behind his desk — channeled his late partner Sgt. John Munch (Richard Belzer, who also portrayed the same character in a 1997 episode of The X-Files) by noting, “It’s just us! Us and the aliens!”

According to NBC’s logline for episode four of season 28, titled “Arcana”: “When a clairvoyant’s account of a nighttime assault raises more questions than answers, Curry must put her skepticism aside to uncover the truth. The squad’s investigation reveals a long-buried secret that has haunted one family for generations.”

Tune in to Law & Order: Special Victims Unit Thursday at 9 p.m. to see if there actually is any supernatural activity at play in the latest case. (The episode will stream on Peacock the following day.)

articles.title: Christina Aguilera Gears Up for ‘Xtinaween’ With X-Rated Bathtub Selfie
articles.author: Hannah Dailey

paras.en: Xtina is putting the “X” in “X-rated” this Halloween. Ahead of the year’s spookiest holiday, Christina Aguilera shared a highly NSFW selfie from her bathtub.

The Instagram photo shared on Wednesday (Oct. 28) shows the pop star standing in her bathtub while snapping the pic in the mirror, which shows her nude reflection. Only two strategically placed thematic ghost emojis cover a bit of skin.
“last looks before xtinaween” Aguilera captioned the picture, adding ghost, jack-o’-lantern and devil emojis.

The caption implies that the five-time Billboard Hot 100-topper has an epic costume teed up, but for now she’s not wearing it (or anything, for that matter) on the ‘gram. Her previous Halloween looks include Cher as Tess in Burlesque — in which Aguilera costarred as Ali — in 2023.
When Xtina does share her look, she’ll join stars such as Paris Hilton, Kim Kardashian, North West, Lizzo, Chloe Bailey and more in taking part in the festivities.

The explicit selfie comes shortly after Aguilera made a surprise appearance at Chappell Roan’s Super Graphic Spectacular show in Los Angeles on Oct. 21, belting out her 2002 smash “Beautiful” before joining the Midwest Princess in duetting on “Coffee.”

“I want to introduce this person [who] honestly paved the way for me and all women in pop to do whatever the f–k they want, sing and wear whatever the f–k they want,” Roan said of Aguilera on stage. “I’m so grateful to have her. She’s a f–king legend.”
The vocalist last dropped a proper studio album, the Spanish-language Aguilera, in 2022, reaching No. 16 on the Billboard Top Latin Pop Albums chart.

articles.title: ‘The Cat in the Hat’ Is Back: How the Seuss Icon’s First Animated Feature Will Kick Off a New Era
articles.author: Lexy Perez

paras.en: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.
In 1957, Theodor Seuss Geisel wrote The Cat in the Hat, a black, white, red, and blue tale about a six-foot whiskered agent of chaos. It disrupted the world of children’s publishing.

“Before there was this very orderly world with our children’s books,” says Susan Brandt, president and CEO of Dr. Seuss Enterprises. “There were Dick and Jane books, and the kids were just impeccable. The Cat disrupted all of that, both in terms of children’s literature and in the story itself. They’re sitting pretty in that window, and he’s like, ‘It’s fun to have fun. You have to know how.’ He challenged us to push boundaries, and to remember that kids are kids.”

In the nearly four decades since Geisel’s passing, the Cat has become the spokesperson of the late author’s library and legacy, despite being published a full 20 years after his first children’s book and debuting the same year as another classic, How the Grinch Stole Christmas. With the theatrical arrival of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s upcoming The Cat in the Hat on Nov. 6 — the first feature-length animated movie starring the titular character — he has the chance to be a disruptor once again.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Starting with live-action, we have a history of that. Our very first film was the 2000 Jim Carrey How the Grinch Stole Christmas, and that was an incredible success,” says Brandt. “Then Chris Meledandri at Illumination came to us and said, ‘I want to do the Grinch.’ I was thinking, we did it. It’s really successful and continues to play well. But he said, ‘I think I can bring a new audience, a new style, a slightly different story.’”

The success of Meledandri‘s animated Grinch film proved to the Dr. Seuss Enterprises head “there was room in the market, and there was room in this story to explore the Cat in a slightly different way,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter. After conversations around town with every major studio, the company chose Warner Bros. Pictures Animation to launch the Cat’s animated feature outing as part of a three-film deal.

At the end of September, while presenting to an eager crowd of animation students as part of the SCAD AnimationFest‘s 10th anniversary, writer-directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni joined head of story Ryan Gaffney and art director Amos Sussigan at the school’s Atlanta campus to tease their new vision of Cat. “I was so impressed by Dr. Seuss Enterprises and Warner Bros. with how much they let us be irreverent,” says Rivinoja. “We were honoring The Cat in the Hat, but we were also having fun with him and his history.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While gathered on the highest floor of the FORTY residence hall, one of the school’s intimate and colorful private event spaces, the team shared elements of the film’s visual production process as they discussed how they’re expanding Geisel’s famous feline in a touching ode to childhood ahead of the story’s 70th anniversary.

“One of the lines in the movie that I love the most is, ‘Childhood is messy.’ I think that’s what the Cat embodies,” Brandt tells The Hollywood Reporter. “Childhood is not sitting pretty. It’s messy, and he creates a safe space for that. I think it’s a beautiful interpretation of the book.”
“And Then Something Went Bump! How That Bump Made Us Jump!”

Since his creation, the Cat has become “a character that’s unlike any other,” says Brandt. For his preschool and kindergarten audience, he’s an approachable figure representing childhood and literacy. Among parents and grandparents, a trusted memory they want to pass on to their children and grandchildren. As the company spokesperson, Cat can be corporate, but also a “chaotic, unexpected, unpredictable ”pop culture figure.”

“This relationship to each demographic is authentic to who he is,” she explains. “They’re all him. So you can take whatever aspect of his personality and see an opportunity. It’s just asking: who are we targeting, and what side of our Cat would we focus on here?”

The film attempted to tap into these multitudes, taking that 60-page book and turning it into a music- and comedy-infused 107-minute adventure that asks “what happens before and after that one location, one day, one tiny set of characters,” according to Rivinoja.

“In the book, it looks like an agent of chaos comes in,” Carloni adds. “But by the time the Cat leaves, they do seem to sit up straighter and appear to be a little more confident. Something changed from when he came in to when he left, and that was enough to make us wonder: Could it be that Cat in the Hat is not just a crazy clown? That he doesn’t only want to have a good time? That maybe he’s someone who’s actually able to find out what a child needs and can give it to them?”

The film’s answer is something not seen in seven decades: an origin story in full color. In Seuss’ black-and-white, hatch-marked version of the real world, readers enter the home of two children when Cat arrives at their front door with two Things in tow. The upcoming movie expands that premise without betraying it, interweaving three animation styles to pay homage to and expand Seuss’ established universe.

Set in that same real world, The Cat in the Hat follows tween Gabby (Xochitl Gomez) and her younger brother Sebastian (Tiago Martinez) after they are left with their goldfish Waffles (Matt Berry) when their mother, Carmen (America Ferrera), has to leave for work. Stuck in their new apartment amid a sea of barely touched moving boxes, Cat emerges from a mouse-sized hole in the wall in all his striped-hatted glory to turn the day around.

In the book, his arrival at the children’s door is inexplicable and spontaneous, but in the film it’s part of a mission to save his job as an agent of entertainment and fun at the I.I.I.I. (Institute for the Institution of Imagination and Inspiration, LLC). “His boss tells him, like we are told often, that he is making a mess, and it’s costing the company too much. If he commits one more mess, he’ll be fired,” Carloni explains. Adds Rivinoja: “The red-and-white hat is how we know the Cat in the Hat. That’s his entire identity. So if he loses that hat, he’s just a regular old cat. That was really a good way of understanding what the stakes are.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: From there, Cat embarks with the kids on an interdimensional journey, moving between the worlds of the apartment and moving boxes as they face down the literal and figurative messes of childhood. “While we were in their apartment, we also needed to go somewhere. We had a film to fill,” says Brandt. “In terms of traditional childhood, appliances came in big boxes, and those boxes became portals for us. The filmmakers picked that up while still being true to this book.”
“It Is Fun to Have Fun, But You Have to Know How“

Before building universes with moving boxes, the team used the book to set a visual tone authentic to and distinct from other Seuss projects for both its real and Seussian worlds. “The real world is more grounded and tangible, but starts changing once the Cat comes,” says Brandt. “That was deliberate and specific. We spent a lot of time talking about how his very presence brings a Seussian feel and things start to warp a little bit.”

Audiences see that as early as the opening sequence, which features the titular character arriving at a familiar house on a rainy afternoon. “It was really important to pay homage to that because it’s the source material,” explains Rivinoja. “[Geisel] was an amazing artist and made such innovative choices in his line work. And once the Cat fully gets the children’s attention, we use color to open up the world.”

Speaking on last month’s SCAD Animation Fest panel, Sussigan expressed that “pitching a studio that you’re going to have an animated movie starting in black and white was a little tough at the beginning.” But “the first few minutes of the movie are to remind the audience where we start and where we go,” Carloni told THR after the panel. “Those colors, it’s the same reason why Superman is red and blue. There was a limitation, especially for the cost at the time. But [Seuss] found this beautiful way to navigate that.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: After coloring in the lives of his latest assignment, the agent of fun travels back to the I.I.I.I., a place Carloni likens to Santa’s North Pole. Visual signatures of Geisel’s style, like negative space and wacky camera angles, abound, with color “oversaturated and your line weights different — a distinct and new look for us,” according to Brandt. Through the Institute, the film reveals that Cat is one of many animal employees, each donning their own red-and-white-striped accessory.

“The most fun that the story crew had early on was just: who are these coworkers?” Gaffney said about dreaming up Cat’s colleagues. “Could it be a raccoon with a spoon? Gopher with loafers? It was populating his little office world and seeing him interact with them.”

With the Institute, the creative team establishes Cat as more than some unwieldy agent of chaos, but a generation-spanning agent of change. “Something that we talked about early on is that chaos is not comedy. It’s not necessarily funny to have someone coming in making a giant mess,” says Rivinoja.

“There’s Santa Claus; there is the Tooth Fairy. We created a mythology where The Cat in the Hat is a character that comes to you in a moment of need in your childhood,” adds Carloni. “A whole institution does this, so if you’re bored one day, you can get Rat with a Bat. Or you can get the best of all because he throws the book out.”

As part of its larger ode to Geisel, the movie also uses the late author’s signature meter, anapestic tetrameter, to create a sort of corporate speak for the whimsical and wacky Institution, while the rest of the film operates in natural dialogue, preserving the voice actors’ styles. “Every time they read some HR documents, it’s in the same metric rhyming,” Carloni explains. “When the boss brings up what Cat has done, he opens up hundreds of Cat in the Hat books we never knew existed, and those are all the same metric rhyming.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Ted Geisel wrote The Cat in the Hat in response to an article in LIFE magazine that asked, ‘Why can’t Johnny read?’ The answer was primers were boring, so why wouldn’t someone like Walt Disney or Dr. Seuss write one?” notes Brandt. “Ted accepted the challenge. There were 250 words that were approved for primers. He used 236 when he wrote The Cat in the Hat. That’s our roots.”
“Then, Fast as a Fox, the Cat in the Hat Came Back in With a Box”

Cat’s Institute and the kids’ real-world styles combine modern animation with original Geisel sensibilities. But the movie’s moving box style invites the visual language to evolve. “From Ted’s first book to 1957 with Cat and Grinch to his last book in 1990, there are variations in style. We have a licensee that does our fine art, and they have traced Ted’s travels to influences on his art. This evolution gives us freedom and flexibility,” says Brandt. “We’ve never done multiple animation styles before in a film, but it’s brilliant because there’s not one style of Seuss. This film embraces that.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “We’ve all seen Spider-Verse. We’ve seen Nimona. We’ve seen the Ninja Turtles. A lot of those movies ask, ‘What if it looked like this?’” Carloni said during the SCAD panel. “But in our movie, we had the opportunity to follow the narrative — from one world we enter into another. We use styles to let viewers know what world we’re navigating between.”

Within those moving boxes, “it’s the idea of what it’s like in a child’s memory and the nostalgia,” says Rivinoja. Color — specifically the book’s classic red and blue — serves as the through line between characters and their growing or thinning emotional connections. Starting in blues, the Cat’s influence seeps in, turning things “more red, but never fully red. For Seb, we go to orange. In Gabby’s, we go all the way to fuchsia,” says Sussigan.

“This is a story about connection and disconnection and everything that’s in between, so we leaned into that when we went into the boxes,” he adds. “It was about understanding how different people understand colors. In Sebastian’s box, we wanted to use colors that were very pure, almost like if he just used a box of 12 crayons. When you go to Gabby’s box, our emotions are a little bit more complex, and so the colors are less pure.”

In the journey between those boxes, a few new Things arrive. “What was so fun was when we decided they don’t all have to look alike,” Rivinoja explains. “Maybe One and Two are just twins, and then we have more. Seuss [Enterprises]was totally on board with that.”

That should come as no surprise, as the Things “are actually one of [Dr. Seuss Enterprises’] biggest merchandise sales,” the writer-director told THR. According to Brandt, the company is already poised to launch their new Things “in market with merchandise,” allowing fans to quickly embrace the Cat’s (in)famous silly sidekicks.

“We [focused on] keeping them deadpan, with no crazy grins, bouncing off each other, with their own way of communicating,” Gaffney says. “We wanted to stay away from Minions territory, but asked what we could do with percussion. The way it happens in the movie, it was so fun to play out their communication in these action set pieces.”

The film playfully winks at the Things potential to win over audiences, and back in 2020, a Thing One and Thing Two film was announced as part of the deal with Warner Bros. Pictures Animation. Its potential plot could possibly be hidden within Cat’s film, but everyone is remaining cautiously optimistic — and vague — about where the Things go next.

“What we’re doing, we’ll see. It is something that we’ll have to sit down with the filmmakers and Bill [Damaschke, president of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation] to say: Is there room for a full movie? I don’t know yet because the storyline hasn’t been established,” says Brandt. “But I think everyone feels it. Let’s learn more about our Things. Why not? I think it could be really fun, and I do think that the Things steal the show a little bit.”
“I Know Some New Tricks … I Will Show Them to You”

Since 1993, Dr. Seuss Enterprises has used Cat across its ventures, from entertainment experiences through Universal’s Islands of Adventure, Broadway, and Carnival Cruise Line to the literacy-focused free book campaigns with First Book and recent publication of the newly uncovered Seuss title Sing the 50 United States!

He’s also led aspects of the company’s expansion from publishing and physical spaces into the digital realm, with mobile apps like the recently launched Dr. Seuss: Learn & Play, YouTube-based Dr. Seuss Babies preschool content, and social media-driven live-action DJ Cat. (The latter has already seen Cat collaborate with Elmo, meme Connor Storrie, dramatically read Pitbull lyrics, and meet his adoring fans on both sides of the DJ table in the most New York way possible.)

Now, with the release of the feature-length animated The Cat in the Hat, the company kicks off an anticipated three-film slate and a year-long celebration of Geisel’s seven decades of influence. “There’s a little bit of an Easter Egg at the end of the film, a nod to what we are calling the 2027 Year of Genius,” says Brandt.

That celebration will start around March 2, as part of an annual celebration of Seuss’ birthday. “We will see Cat on the floor with our books. You’ll see our merchandise. You should see a nice burst of a campaign talking about our Genius Year,” the CEO explains. “Seuss is all about celebrating the uniqueness and possibilities within each one of us. We want to acknowledge the genius that was Ted, the genius that are these characters, and the genius that’s within each of us.”

That will be followed by several activations “where we pop up in what we think are genius ways and moments with partners,” Brandt tells THR. During the 70th anniversary summer, the company will bring together two of its icons — Cat and the Grinch — for the first time in the company’s history. The fourth quarter will focus on the Grinch, with something in between that the company can’t yet reveal.

Alongside the new film slate and Year of Genius celebration, the company is working to expand its location-based experiences. “We work with a group, WildBrain CPLG, that helps us think through more theme park opportunities,” says Brandt. “The LBE space for Cat and our other characters — whether it’s Lorax, Green Eggs and Ham, Horton, or our Fish — that’s a really interesting area that we’re exploring. There are conversations and partnerships, you can hear it in my smile, that we are on the cusp of announcing.”

paras.en: All of this will help launch the next era of a global entertainment empire built on books. It’s a chapter that will feature the upcoming Jon M. Chu-directed Oh, the Places You’ll Go!, a film Brandt describes as “definitely a musical” where the soundtrack is going “to be emotional, important” and at the “forefront of the storytelling” — versus The Cat in the Hat, where a marching band version of Taylor Swift’s “Shake It Off” and a new track from Hilary Duff “serve as a vehicle to take you someplace with your emotions,” she says.

paras.en: With the release of The Cat in the Hat, the iconic character is primed to help the company continue to honor its literary roots and spirit of expansion for the next generation. “Ted did the first stage show for The 500 Hats of Bartholomew Cubbins. He did a film, The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T. He did merchandise. He had the Grinch Christmas television show, which he himself, even then, had to take and give backstory and breath,” says Brandt. “If you’re going to take these beautiful books, their characters and messages, and create other projects with them, you have to allow some freedom and flexibility, and I see permission to do so from Ted Geisel himself.”

articles.title: Universal Music Group Posts $3.78 Billion in Revenue For Q3, Signals Fight Against AI Slop
articles.author: Ethan Millman

paras.en: Universal Music Group posted 3.394 billion euros (about $3.78 billion) in revenue in its third quarter, the world’s largest record company said in its quarterly earnings report published Thursday, a nearly 12 percent increase from 2025.

Recorded revenue grew just over 7 percent excluding revenue from its acquisition of Downtown Music and nearly 15 percent overall, up to 2.55 billion euros or $2.84 billion. Music publishing revenue grew 7.5 percent, or about 1.5 percent when excluding the Downtown revenue, up to 590 million euros or about $659 million. On the company’s earnings call Thursday, Chairman and CEO Lucian Grainge called the Downtown acquisition “the most important acquisition UMG has made since EMI.”

UMG cited releases from Mrs. Green Apple, Olivia Rodrigo, Stray Kids, Ariana Grande and The Beatles as among the biggest performers this quarter. Subscription revenue grew to about $2 billion, an 18 percent jump from last year, with an eight percent growth when excluding downtown. Physical revenue jumped 15 percent at 392 million euros, or about $437 million.

“Our results show the enduring value of backing extraordinary artists, bold ideas, and the teams and technology that help bring their work to the world,” Grainge said in a statement. “The industry is healthy and growing, and we will keep evolving from a position of strength. We are investing in human artistry, improving the economics of streaming, and expanding what’s possible for artists and fans. To support that strategy, we are making UMG faster and more focused so we can operate more efficiently and drive sustained growth and long-term value.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Merchandise revenue fell about 4.6 percent this quarter, attributable to fewer major tours, coming in at 248 million euros, or about $277 million.

UMG’s earnings report comes two weeks after the company underwent a notable round of layoffs that also include notable executive departures including Def Jam CEO Tunji Balogun and Republic Records chief Jim Roppo, as well as several executives at Interscope.

During the earnings call, Grainge spent much of his opening comments discussing AI and the efforts UMG and other industry stakeholders including streaming platforms have taken thus far to combat the proliferation of AI slop. Grainge had said that the “scale of the problem outpaces the progress,” giving an example of the blues charts “being polluted with AI content that synthetically imitates that emotional impact.”
“AI slop degrades the fan experience and diverts value from real artists. It serves no one. Not artists, platforms or consumers,” Grainge said.
He advocated for AI slop to be paid out less than music from actual musicians to disincentivize “industrial scale content production.”

articles.title: People Inc. Cuts 195 Staffers Over “Rapid Changes” In Media
articles.author: Erik Hayden

paras.en: In the second major round of layoffs this year, Barry Diller‘s magazine empire is reorganizing over what it describes as a “rapid” transformation in the media landscape.

His company, People Inc., is cutting 195 staffers primarily in print and website departments, a memo from CEO Neil Vogel to staff stated on Thursday. The firm, formerly titled IAC up until a rebrand this year that emphasizes its flagship title, houses People, InStyle, Food & Wine, Travel + Leisure, Southern Living and Entertainment Weekly and holds significant minority stakes in MGM Resorts and car rental marketplace Turo. The company had 5,156 employees as of its latest 10-K filing last December.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “The rapid changes in media are evident to us all, and require us to be constantly changing as well. We have significantly increased investments in a host of new projects as we continue to align the company with our biggest opportunities,” wrote CEO Vogel in the note to employees. “The vast majority of those affected today are in our print and legacy web businesses, as we continue to evolve for a prosperous future.”

Vogel added that the company has added 320 new employees this year “and we plan to continue making meaningful investments in 2027.” The company plans to have an all-hands meeting to discuss its path forward after People Inc. discloses its quarterly earnings on Nov. 3.

Recently the CEO had described a shift in People Inc.’s business to reorient it from dependence on Google web traffic. “The Google risk is out of the business,” Vogel told a Goldman Sachs investor conference in September. “It’s down to 20 percent of our just web audience, and we’ve built these really diverse audiences and really diverse revenue streams across some of the best brands in the world, and we’re a very strong and healthy business where we sit right now.”

In April, when IAC formally rebranded as People Inc., the company said in a regulatory filing company it would undergo a restructuring that included staff layoffs in order to find an annual savings of $40 million when it was done with the overhaul.

The move arrives a day after People Inc. and MGM Resorts appear to have ended their tie-up talks. Diller’s firm had pursued an $18 billion takeover bid earlier this year in June. It then dropped the bid in September, and MGM then appeared to be pursuing People Inc. A new voting agreement restricts People Inc. from purchasing additional shares once its ownership stake reaches 29.9 percent.

When Diller played his cards for MGM Resorts in June he characterized the attempt to buy a majority stake in the Bellagio owner as a big bet on resorts, casinos and experiences being an “AI proof” proposition for consumers. Unlike, say, some aspects of the media landscape that relies on the open web.

But that bid appears to be in the rearview now. “The discussion between MGM and People ends there,” said MGM Resorts CEO Bill Hornbuckle in a call with analysts on Wednesday. “Management continues to be focused on the business as clear and consistent.”

articles.title: Third-quarter U.S. GDP increases a better-than-expected 3.4% as September inflation accelerates

paras.en: The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday.

The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below.

Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends.
While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter.
GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter.
Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%.

The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move.
"The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.
However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do.

A Labor Department report also released Thursday showed that layoffs remain low. Initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the estimate for 200,000 and near levels last seen in the late 1960s.
Stock market futures were negative following the releases while Treasury yields also fell.

"Net, net, economic growth is powering ahead despite the uncertainty of geopolitical risks and the damage posed to many sectors of the economy by higher energy costs," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "The economy was thought to have been a lost cause during much of the current Administration's time in office, but real GDP has bounced back above a 3 percent run rate in Q3 2026 for the first time in a year."
Economic growth has been driven by higher levels of investment from the artificial intelligence build-out, as well as high levels of consumer and government spending.

Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products.
Real sales to private domestic purchasers, a proxy that Fed officials use for underlying demand, rose 4.9%, compared with a 4.6% increase in the second quarter.
There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter.

September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%.
At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

articles.title: Big Oil earnings are set to surge. Why investors may want to be cautious

paras.en: That's not a reference to the reportedly amazing new documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. It's about the next few days and next week: days that will be dominated by earnings, a massive conference, and more on Europe's energy woes.
I'll hit more on energy earnings in The Actionable Insider below.

Next week for me, it's multiple flights through multiple time zones. First up is one of the most important energy conferences in the world: ADIPEC in Abu Dhabi. It's a who's who of the energy world. I'll be speaking with some of the most influential energy executives in the world. You'll see some clips on CNBC about it and then I'll write about it here next week. I'll also be meeting privately with some of the biggest power players in energy and having great conversations with country and company leaders about oil, gas, commodities, Hormuz, and more - all ahead of what some fear may be another round of hits on Iran or Iranian energy infrastructure. It remains a tense time.

paras.en: That will be followed later in the week by a deeper dive into Europe's slow-rolling energy crisis. The Iran war and Hormuz risk have added another layer to an already risky situation, but let's be clear: it is not the reason why Europe is in an energy bind. Russia's horrible invasion and now four-year war on Ukraine added gasoline to a fire that began burning with bad policy decisions years ago. I have been covering the European energy story for five years - from the UK, Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands - and next week I'll be in Italy highlighting where Europe is right now. Hint: it's not good. Natural gas storage levels are below their recent average, and prices are near record highs for imported LNG.

Speaking of the Middle East, on my X account I posted a rather blurry picture sent by a friend of mine in Dubai a few days ago. On a morning swim, he spotted a U.S. Navy ship standing guard in the distance in the Arabian (Persian) Gulf. It's blurry because he had to zoom in from a distance, but regardless, I think it tells a thousand words. Oil is flowing through Hormuz in part because the great U.S. Navy is making sure ships get through. This ship and the brave men and women on it are part of that. But there's also the risk that the Iran war heats back up, with new U.S. assaults on Iranian targets. If that happens, oil is likely to pop. We live in a day-to-day, or even hour-by-hour, world.
