articles.title: Big cats, unexplained lights and a floodlit eclipse — 7 skywatching 'horror stories' to keep you entertained this Halloween
articles.author: Anthony Wood

paras.en: Halloween is almost upon us! To celebrate we've pulled together a series of short "skywatching horror stories" perfect for getting you in the mood for the spooky season.

Granted, stargazing may not be the most hazardous of past times. But you'd be surprised how often things can go wrong. The best laid plans can be shattered by the unforeseen, unexpected phenomena can leave you scared witless, or mother nature itself can step in to remind us how little control we have over the environment around us.

Many of the stories serve as a cautionary tale, while others are simply..unfortunate. Be sure to share your stories of skywatching "horror stories" in the comments below for a chance to feature in next year's Halloween coverage!
And how better to kick off our Halloween skywatching tales than with a retelling of the strange event that terrified my entire family during a trip to France, two decades ago.
We had rented a house in the Charente, with few neighbors and no city lights. It was a stargazer's paradise, so each night we would sit outside as dusk's light faded to twilight.

One night, we stood transfixed as an electrical storm conjured sheet lightning in the distance, when without warning a shining ball of light burst into being on the near horizon. We watched, unsettled as the yellow-red light gently descended behind a row of oaks before passing over the nearby field.

My mom fled inside, convinced that we'd seen a UFO, while my dad and brothers stood and watched as the light silently flitted between the trees before disappearing from sight around five minutes after it had appeared.

We were alone in the darkness, trying to make sense of what we'd seen when a rustle in the bushes had us borderline sprinting inside, all pretences of bravery gone and images of alien greys in our heads.

Our best guess is that we saw some kind of rare electrical phenomenon that night, like ball lightning, which has been reported over 10,000 times throughout recorded history but is still very poorly understood.
My mom maintains that we narrowly avoided being abducted.

Our next entry comes from Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic, who traveled all the way from the U.K. to the U.S. in the hope of seeing her first total solar eclipse, only to have totality ruined by a series of extremely unfortunate events!

"My first-ever total solar eclipse experience in Rochester, New York, on April 8, 2024, was memorable for all the wrong reasons, Dobrijovic explained. "I was attending the Rochester Museum & Science Center's ROC the Eclipse Festival, where thick clouds had completely obscured the sun. But even without seeing the eclipse itself, totality was extraordinary.

An ominous darkness raced across the sky, while rusty-red hues illuminated the clouds, creating an almost apocalyptic scene. The clouds looked as though they'd been lifted straight from a Renaissance painting. The atmosphere was electric as thousands of excited spectators watched daylight disappear. We couldn't see the eclipse, but we could certainly feel it.

Then, about 30 seconds into totality, disaster struck. We were standing in the museum's car park when the security floodlights suddenly flickered on, automatically triggered by the darkness. The harsh artificial lighting completely shattered the otherworldly atmosphere, robbing us of our chance to experience totality's eerie darkness.

Thousands of spectators erupted into boos, shouting, 'Turn off the lights!' After traveling thousands of miles for my first total solar eclipse, I'd been thwarted first by clouds, then by a car park's security lights. Talk about adding insult to injury!"
Astrophotographer Dan Bartlett experienced a very different skywatching horror story after preparing his telescopes for a night of astrophotography at his home in the Eastern Sierra Mountains.

Nature had other plans. A security camera captured the sickening moment that an unexpected and sustained deluge of 77-mile-per-hour winds toppled Bartlett's Celestron Rowe-AckermannAstrograph 11-inch and 8-inch telescopes, mounts, accessories and all.
"A telescope owner's worst nightmare…Equal to dropping a prized eyepiece or telescope on a cement/concrete ground," Bartlett remonstrated with Space.com.

"When you first see the two scopes lying side by side, no longer upright, your reaction is to stand there and stare. Quick action of prevention is well past its timeliness. Eventually you start to pick things up and assess the damage."

"One might [put] me at fault for not taking down the scopes prior, and rightly so, however the scopes have survived sustained winds of 60+ mph winds over and over before," continued Bartlett. "You develop a level of complacency and no weather forecast in the days of the event predicted winds as high as was recorded.
Damage done? Severe. At least the dented tube of the RASA 11 has continued to win NASA APOD after APOD since the event. Oh, I now use sandbags on a heavier mount."
Bartlett continues to capture spectacular images of the night sky to this day.

High winds may be a potent adversary for the humble stargazer, but you know what else can complicate things? Literal mountain Lions, which is what American Meteor Society shooting star expert Robert Lunsford came face to face with on a stargazing outing to the western slope of Mt. Laguna, California.

"I was viewing alone in the local mountains many years ago," Lunsford recounted to Space.com. "Back then I often heard what I thought were juvenile mountain lions screeching in the dark. They were never too close until one night I shone my flashlight upon a full-grown cat about fifty yards away."

"The adrenalin was flowing big time as I kept that light on it. Luckily, it decided it wanted no part of me and headed back down the hill. Ever since then when viewing alone I sit in the bed of my truck to offer a little more sense of security."

Lunsford's cautionary tale serves as a potent reminder that you should always tell a friend or family member when you head somewhere remote for a spot of stargazing. And that you should probably do a little research on the local flora and fauna before making the trip!

Royal Observatory Greenwich astronomer Gideon Bendavid-Walker had a run in with nature at a very different scale while leading a stargazing tour through the Arkaroola Wilderness Sanctuary in the South Australian outback, under some of the darkest skies on Earth.

"I was running a tour from the sparsely used 1980's Dodwell Observatory as our main telescope was out for maintenance," Bendavid-Walker shared with Space.com. "It was going beautifully. I was out in the dark with my laser pointer, guiding a rapt group around the southern sky, when I felt a nip at my ankle. Then another.

I quickly discovered that I was standing on a meat ant nest. By day they're easy to spot: a little circle of gravelly sand with a hole in the middle. At night, they're invisible, and meat ants do not take kindly to their nests being stood on."

For those of us unfamiliar with the Australian Outback, meat ants are known for being aggressive towards any they deem an intruder, have a nasty bite and are named for their habit of stripping the flesh from dead animals.

"Mid-constellation, I abandoned the cosmos and began hopping, slapping and yelling into the night. My startled guests rallied heroically, flooding the scene with torchlight (a cardinal sin for dark-adapted eyes, but quickly forgiven) and helping me evict the invaders.
My dignity stayed behind with the ants."
The moral of the story — try to look down before looking up, it may save your ankles.

There's a long and storied tradition of nature having its fun with astronomers, as proven by Arthur S. Eddington's complication-filled trip to West Africa, as told by Louise Devoy, Senior Curator at Royal Observatory Greenwich.

"What a nightmare....Cambridge astronomer Arthur S. Eddington watched anxiously as the skies over Principe, West Africa, clouded over with thunderous storms," Devon explained to Space.com. "As a Quaker Christian, he'd narrowly avoided jail for avoiding military service during the First World War, thanks to the intervention of Frank Dyson, the Astronomer Royal at Greenwich.

Dyson knew that Eddington was the best person to use the imminent total solar eclipse as a test of Einstein's 1915 theory of general relativity. Eddington and his colleague Edwin T. Cottingham had travelled thousands of miles to secure the best view but their plans were thwarted by every eclipse chaser's nightmare: thunderstorms, pesky mosquitoes and mischievous monkeys from the surrounding jungle who enjoyed tampering with the instruments.

Eddington and his colleague Cottingham only managed to secure one decent photograph through thin cloud. Thankfully, their Greenwich colleagues Charles Davidson and Andrew Crommelin at Sobral, northern Brazil, had better luck and their photographs confirmed Einstein's prediction."

Our final tale of stargazing misfortune comes from award-winning landscape astrophotographer Josh Dury, who found himself in a race against time to stage a recreation of a famous scene from television history, with a Milky Way twist.

"One that comes to mind was the image I captured, titled: "Boy on Bike". The purpose of the image was to re-enact the classic scene from Ridley Scott's 1973 Hovis Advert through the lens of Astrophotography. I was hoping an assistant could model with the bike but plans collapsed, so I decided to do it myself.

Earlier that day, I had collected the bike from a local seller and purchased bread to resemble Hovis loaves. Driving to location in a 4x4 — bike in trailer, I dressed in outfit and progressed to Gold Hill.

Arriving before 2 a.m., there were bright LED lights still on. I had to wait until every single one turned off but one. I had to somehow get the bike into position on the steep hill, obtain focus and prepare the other elements — including a lamp and arranging the bread basket.
With the Milky Way moving into place, I really did not have much time. Setting up a star tracker and a prop set at the same time was a significant challenge.
Then, the epic finale. The weight of the lamp outbalanced the bike and collapsed with the most almighty thud (wheels still spinning). I could see lights in the street turning on!! I was mortified."

If these horror stories haven't totally put you off and you're interested in starting out on your own stargazing journey then be sure to read our expert tips for newcomers to the night sky, along with our picks of the best telescopes and binoculars for exploring the post-sunset realm.
Editor's Note: If you would like to share your astrophotography with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

articles.title: Cosmic graveyard of zombie planets offers a grisly warning about our own solar system's fate
articles.author: Robert Lea

paras.en: "Sometimes dead is better." Who can forget the immortal words of Jud Crandall, delivered by the incomparable Fred Gwynne in the 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's Pet Sematary? Turns out Crandall could have been talking about somewhere just as otherworldly as the cursed Chumash burial ground at the heart of one of King's most terrifying works of fiction.

That's because astronomers have discovered two husks of two zombie planets shuffling through the gory remains of what was once their planetary neighbors around a long-deceased star, or white dwarf. The shattered planets were revealed by a clear gap in the debris around the white dwarf J1328−1450, located around 1,600 light-years away from Earth. One of the remnants is estimated to be no larger than the size of the average solar system asteroid, while the other is estimated to be between the size of the moon and the dwarf planet Pluto.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If this wasn't creepy enough, this haunting planetary system could be a grisly warning about the future of our own solar system after the inevitable death of the sun.

White dwarfs like the one at the heart of this system are formed when stars around the same mass as the sun run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means they can no longer fuse hydrogen into helium, the nuclear fusion process that provides the outward push that supports a star against the inward push of its own gravity.

As a result, the stars' cores collapse while the outer layers, where nuclear fusion is still proceeding, puff out. This so-called red giant phase can see stars increase their radius by many 100s of times. When it happens to the sun in around 5 billion years, our star will expand to consume the inner planets, including Earth.

The red giant phase ends when the outer layers disperse along with the wreckage of consumed planets, leaving a smoldering stellar core, now a white dwarf, surrounded by the disk-shaped remains of its outer layers and cannibalized planetary children. But this may not be the final death of all the planets that once orbited the now-dead star.

"We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals," research leader Nicola Gentille Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste, Italy, said in a statement.
Violent stellar death can't kill these two planetary Jason Voorhees

This system differs from others seen because of the large gap between the remarkably stable inner and outer rings. All previously known debris discs around white dwarfs have been surrounded by single, flat, rotating disks, not a double structure like this.

"The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized," team member Gentle Fusillo of the Astronomical Observatory of Trieste said.
The team thinks that this unique double structure is evidence of planets that weren't completely vaporized during this white dwarf's red giant phase.
That means just like the residents and campers of Crystal Lake couldn't finish off Pamela Voorhees' baby boy, even an expanding star couldn't finish these two planets.

The team's observations, made with the Very Large Telescope (VLT), revealed the presence of calcium, oxygen, magnesium, and iron in the disk around the white dwarf. This indicates the destroyed planets had a composition similar to the rocky planets of the inner solar system.

The researchers also found evidence of a diversity of composition in the destroyed planets. The chemistry of the outer rings deviated from that of the inner rings, indicating that at least two of the consumed planets had very different compositions.
"The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like," Lagos-Vilches explained.
The team's research was published on Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

articles.title: TechnoMile Recognized as a 2026 Inc. Power Partner Award Winner

paras.en: TechnoMile, the leading AI solution that unifies growth, contracts, compliance, and security workflows, has been named a 2026 Inc. Power Partner Awards winner, recognizing the company among the leading B2B partners supporting entrepreneurs and businesses across the country.

The annual Inc. Power Partner Awards honor B2B companies that have demonstrated a track record of helping entrepreneurs and businesses navigate the challenges of building and growing a company. TechnoMile’s unified platform connects growth, contracts, and security workflows, delivering GovCon, Defense, and Public Sector organizations greater visibility, stronger compliance, lower risk, and more efficient operations. By combining purpose-built technology, trusted AI, and deep government contracting experience, TechnoMile helps organizations compete for, win, and successfully execute mission-critical government work.

“TechnoMile solves a real problem for the contracting market – providing a unified way to manage the full lifecycle of federal business,” said Ashish Khot, CEO of TechnoMile. “This award is a special honor because it is largely based on the feedback and experience of our customers and shows that we are living up to our promise to be a partner for business growth, helping companies better manage the work behind winning and delivering federal business.”

articles.title: Craft Prospect kicks off PERSEUS project to advance optical communications for space
articles.author: Craft Prospect

paras.en: Craft Prospect is working with Fraunhofer Centre for Applied Photonics (Fraunhofer CAP) and Vector Photonics on a new project exploring the potential of next-generation laser technology for high-performance optical communications in space.

PERSEUS (PCSEL Environmental and Radiation Sensitivity: Evaluation for Use in Space) will investigate whether a promising new laser technology called Photonic-Crystal Surface-Emitting Lasers (PCSELs) is suitable for operation in space and can offer a differentiated capability for both space-to-space and space/ground networks.

The project will evaluate the technology under conditions relevant to space deployment, demonstrate its compatibility with representative spacecraft hardware, and identify the next engineering steps required to move towards a commercial solution.

The project is funded through the Advanced Connectivity Technologies (ACT) programme, delivered by Innovate UK and funded by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The ACT R&D Programme was announced by Minister Ian Murray during his speech at Connected Britain on 9 September 2026.
Exploring a new approach to optical communications

PCSEL technology offers the potential to address some of the limitations of existing optical and RF communications systems in space, supporting the move towards longer-range, higher-capacity, and more secure free-space optical links between ground stations, satellites, and potentially deeper-space assets.
By bridging the gap between component and space system, PERSEUS will chart a course from disruptive technology to differentiated on-orbit capability for the fast-growing space market.
From device testing to spacecraft integration

The PERSEUS programme will subject PCSELs to a range of test campaigns expected of space qualified technologies, as well as carrying out long-range, high-bandwidth free-space demonstrations to showcase early performance.

PCSEL devices will undergo characterisation and testing, including radiation, vibration, and thermal-vacuum campaigns, to better our understanding of how the technology fares in the launch and space environments.

Furthermore, the project will demonstrate early integration success with other flight-representative hardware for end-to-end data transmission, and develop mission concepts that harness the unique capabilities of PCSELs.

The findings will feed into a future communications system design concept and help define the engineering roadmap required to progress PCSEL technology towards a differentiated space communications solution.
Bringing together photonics and space engineering expertise
At Craft Prospect, Head of Engineering Kevin Quillien is serving as Project Lead, supported by Chief Engineer Paul Yarr and Systems Engineers Lauryn Atkinson and Kairavi Pandit.
At Fraunhofer CAP, Dr Gerald Bonner is subcontract lead, while at Vector Photonics Dr Richard Taylor serves as subcontract lead and Dr Graham Goldberg as Project Manager.

The project also builds on Craft Prospect’s growing quantum-optical communications capability, including our work on OPS-SAT VOLT, where we are developing and testing space-to-ground free-space quantum and optical communications technologies as part of our wider mission to deliver Smart Secure Space.
Kevin Quillien, Project Lead and Head of Engineering Craft Prospect, said of the project:
‘PERSEUS is an exciting opportunity to take a promising new photonics technology and understand the potential it has to offer the space industry.

‘By carrying out all the necessary early-stage work to test and characterise PCSELs for space, we will build a strong understanding of the potential that the technology offers in building the next generation of communication solutions. We’re looking forward to working with Fraunhofer CAP and Vector Photonics to explore where this roadmap will take us.’

Craft Prospect is a Glasgow-based space engineering company advancing its vision of Smart Secure Space through onboard intelligence, quantum technologies, and satellite subsystem innovation. Learn more here.
About Fraunhofer Centre for Applied Photonics

Fraunhofer CAP is a not-for-profit research and technology organisation (RTO) offering industry a professional development capability in the fields of photonics, lasers and quantum technologies. Learn more about Fraunhofer CAP here.

Vector Photonics Limited, based in Glasgow, is advancing its revolutionary, proprietary, PCSEL technology from proven R&D and commercial fab environments to high-volume manufacturing. Further information can be found here

articles.title: NIH–NASA QuSAFE Challenge
articles.author: Bailey Light

paras.en: The Quantum-Enabled Predictive Preclinical NAMs for Toxicity and Safety (QuSAFE) Challenge, a collaboration between the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and NASA, advances quantum-enabled sensing for in vitro NAMs, such as organoids and microphysiological systems (MPS), to improve drug safety while reducing animal use.

In vitro NAMs, such as organoids and microphysiological systems (MPS), can generate human-relevant data for drug development and safety evaluation. However, conventional assays and imaging are often noisy, invasive, and not sensitive enough. As a result, weak, early, and low-abundance biological signals can go undetected, and destructive measurements make it hard to monitor dynamic processes over time. Quantum-enabled sensing approaches can offer ultra-high sensitivity, improved signal-to-noise performance, and nanoscale resolution, overcoming detection and measurement limitations that today’s approaches can’t reach.

paras.en: The NIH-NASA QuSAFE Challenge directly supports NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division, addressing the need for advanced detection methods that work beyond traditional labs.
By leveraging recent advances in sensor-development research communities, the challenge enhances NASA’s space exploration capabilities and benefits science both in space and on Earth.

articles.title: NASA Names Troy Asher Armstrong Flight Research Center Director
articles.author: Lauren E. Low

paras.en: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Troy Asher director of the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Asher, a veteran test pilot and aerospace engineer with decades of experience in flight research and operations, has served as the center’s acting director since March.

“Troy has spent his career pushing the boundaries of flight, both at the controls of experimental aircraft and leading the teams that make these missions possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “He understands what it takes to turn ambitious ideas into successful flight tests, and his experience will be invaluable as Armstrong leads the way in rebuilding NASA’s X-plane portfolio, restoring our flight-test capabilities, and flying higher, farther, and faster than we have in decades.”

“Flight testing demands a rare combination of technical excellence, operational judgment, and trust in the teams that make every mission possible,” said NASA Associate Administrator and Chief Engineer Amit Kshatriya. “Troy’s service to America, from his distinguished career as an Air Force test pilot to his leadership of some of NASA’s most challenging flight research missions, embodies those qualities. Few people better understand the art and discipline of flight testing, and he brings a deep understanding of both the aircraft and the teams behind every successful mission. As director, Troy will help us revolutionize how we develop, evaluate, and fly new technologies, strengthening the capabilities that keep NASA at the forefront of aerospace research.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Asher will oversee Armstrong’s workforce and operations, leading NASA’s efforts to advance flight research, aircraft operations, and the development of new aviation technologies. As NASA’s Flight Test and Aircraft Operations Center of Excellence, Armstrong plays a central role in the agency’s efforts to rebuild and expand its X-plane portfolio, pushing the boundaries of high-speed flight and developing experimental aircraft and technologies that will shape the future of aviation. The center also supports airborne science missions and flight research across the agency.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Prior to becoming acting center director, Asher served as director of Flight Operations at Armstrong, overseeing the center’s pilots, engineers, maintainers, and fleet of specialized aircraft supporting aeronautics research and scientific missions around the world.

Asher joined NASA in 2008 as a research test pilot and aerospace engineer. During his time as a NASA pilot, he conducted flight research aboard aircraft, including the F-15, F/A-18, Gulfstream III, and X-56A unmanned aircraft system. He served as the lead test pilot for the development of NASA’s Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA) and flew scientific research missions aboard the agency’s DC-8 aircraft, supporting airborne science campaigns around the globe.

Before joining NASA, Asher completed a 24-year career in the U.S. Air Force, retiring as a lieutenant colonel. His military service included assignments as an instructor at the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School at Edwards Air Force Base, commander of the 419th Flight Test Squadron, and director of the Bomber Combined Test Force. In 2003, he set 25 world speed records flying the B-1B bomber.
Asher earned a bachelor’s degree in astronautical engineering from the U.S. Air Force Academy and a master’s degree in mechanical engineering from California State University, Fresno.
Asher succeeds Bradley Flick, who retired in March following nearly 40 years of NASA service.

Established in 1946, Armstrong has been at the forefront of American flight research for eight decades, from the first supersonic flight aboard the Bell X-1 to today’s work advancing quiet supersonic flight through NASA’s X-59 aircraft. The center continues to push the boundaries of aviation while providing critical flight research and operational capabilities in support of NASA’s science, technology, and exploration missions.
For more information about NASA Armstrong, visit:
Armstrong Flight Research Center, Edwards, Calif.

articles.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
articles.author: Amanda Barnett

paras.en: When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found. Named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, the meteorite is one of roughly 435 from the Red Planet.

In a paper published Thursday in Science, researchers offered an initial characterization of Teghaza 001, providing a rare snapshot of Mars’ ancient crust and formation. What scientists learn from future studies could help answer many questions, including how water and rocks interacted on ancient Mars. A separate paper published in Science Advances in June detailed the meteorite’s water content, offering a look at how water shaped the early planet’s surface.

“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” said the paper’s lead author, Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars.”

What sets Teghaza 001 apart from other Martian meteorites is its texture and age as well as the uniqueness of its igneous, or volcanic, minerals. It is one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth. While invaluable, the others provide more limited glimpses of Mars’ geological history. They include ALH84001, which is composed almost entirely of one mineral and is similar in age to Teghaza 001. The other meteorite, nicknamed “Black Beauty,” formed about 2.1 billion years ago and is composed of small, volcanic rock fragments.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Unlike its ancient peers, Teghaza 001 has a mix of igneous minerals that tells a story about how the planet’s crust formed from cooling magma before it was eventually altered by subsurface water. The meteorite’s distinctive mineralogy matches what NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has observed in the planet’s cratered southern highlands. No one will ever know exactly where the meteorite originated on Mars, but the paper identifies several potential locations that match Teghaza 001’s mineralogy and chemistry.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” said the new paper’s second author, Lee Saper, who conducted the research while at JPL as a postdoctoral scholar. Lee now is a scientist at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley. “It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water.”

Although the Mars meteorites found on Earth differ from one another, they share a common history, having been blasted off the Red Planet’s surface by an impact, followed by a trajectory that eventually placed them on Earth and into the hands of scientists. Meteorites are often found by collectors in deserts or snowy plains, where they stand out from the rest of the barren landscape. Scientists can verify a meteorite as Martian by matching its mineral and chemical components to data collected by NASA’s Mars missions, including the Viking landers as well as the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When Liu was first asked to look at Teghaza 001, she almost passed on the opportunity.

Researchers at the University of New Mexico had already identified it as Martian based on its oxygen isotopes, which serve as geochemical fingerprints for different planetary bodies. In this case, the researchers matched the meteorite’s oxygen isotopes to those seen in other Martian meteorites. Teghaza 001 appeared to be a shergottite which is the most common class of meteorite from the Red Planet. As an expert in planetary samples, Liu has seen plenty of those, but she decided to take a peek, anyway.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: At the very least, there were odd textures and unusual minerals she hadn’t seen before. Liu and her colleagues discovered zircon crystals in Teghaza 001, which record clues to a rock’s formation and can be used by geologists to precisely age-date a sample. Further analysis revealed when Teghaza 001 formed and when certain changes, like water alteration, occurred.

Caltech coauthor Francois Tissot helped the researchers utilize a novel age-dating method pioneered by his team. Compared with bulk-analysis techniques, where a sample is entirely dissolved and analyzed, Tissot’s in-situ rubidium-strontium age-dating used a piece of Teghaza 001 that was smaller than a fingernail, analyzing single mineral grains on its surface. Besides its extreme precision and speed, the technique preserves rare samples like Martian meteorites for future studies.

“Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite,” Tissot said. “Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from other planets, their moons, and asteroids.”

When the age-dating results came back, Liu was shocked: This rock had been altered by Martian water sometime around 4.1 billion years ago, suggesting it originally formed even earlier. Clues within the oxygen isotopes, texture, and chemistry of Teghaza 001 minerals point to a much more dynamic water cycle on early Mars.
This year’s papers are just the start. Liu and her co-authors are eager to see what the rest of the scientific community can learn from Teghaza 001.
“We’ve only scratched the surface,” Liu said.
Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif.

articles.title: Nature is making a comeback – now restoration funding must quadruple

paras.en: Nature is making a comeback – now restoration funding must quadruple

Some 252 million hectares across 149 countries – an area of land and sea roughly the size of Kazakhstan – are currently under restoration, making this the largest documented effort of its kind to date. More than one million green jobs have also been created in the process.
“Today, we are witnessing the makings of one of the largest movements for nature in recorded history,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
However, more action is needed to meet global restoration targets, UNEP and sister agencies said in a report launched on Thursday at the COP17 biodiversity conference in Yerevan, Armenia.
Nature’s comeback - Scaling ecosystem restoration for people and planet comes at the halfway point for the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, which runs through 2030.

The report assesses progress on a global commitment to restore around one billion hectares of land – roughly the size of China – by the end of this period and ensure that 30 per cent of the world’s ecosystems are under conservation, in line with a 2022 agreement known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

For this to happen there must be rapid acceleration, particularly in freshwater, marine and coastal ecosystems. Annual funding for restoration also needs to increase more than fourfold from $64 billion to $296 billion – an investment that could create up to 32 million jobs worldwide by 2030.

“Five years into the UN Decade, the message is clear: restoration works,” said Dongyu Qu, Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), which co-published the report alongside UNEP and the UN biodiversity secretariat.
“The challenges are to make restoration an integral part of the sustainable management of land, water and natural resources, and to have a coherent transformation of agrifood systems.”
Helping nature to bounce back is essential for food and water security, climate resilience, jobs and wellbeing.

Research suggests that restoring just 15 per cent of global priority areas could prevent 60 per cent of projected species extinctions while 30 per cent of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions could also be sequestered.

Yet progress is variable across ecosystems and countries. For example, restoration of terrestrial ecosystems has reached nearly half the 30 per cent target, but marine and coastal restoration has been far more limited.
The report said restoration must be sustained long enough to both enable ecosystem and biodiversity recovery while delivering lasting benefits for communities.
“We cannot expect to fix nature with one hand while we destroy it with the other one,” said Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Secretariat.
“Governments must address the drivers of ecosystem degradation and invest in monitoring mechanisms to ensure the durability of the restoration movement to date.”

articles.title: Russia drone strike on Ukrainian railway station kills 13

paras.en: Russia drone strike on Ukrainian railway station kills 13

“Civilians preparing for a trip, welcoming or bidding farewell to loved ones faced death and devastation,” said Matthias Schmale, the Humanitarian Coordinator for Ukraine, adding that displaced people and humanitarian workers at a transit centre at the station were left in shock by the nearby explosions.

Media outlets reported that a jet-powered drone hit the station as a train due to travel to Zaporizhzhia stood at a platform. An 11-year-old boy was among the injured, according to regional officials cited in the reports.
Mr. Schmale expressed condolences to the families of those killed on behalf of the UN, noting that train travel is a key means of transportation in Ukraine.

Since the start of the year, he said, travellers and railway workers have faced increased risks on every journey due to Russian military strikes and air alerts affecting the safety and reliability of trains.
According to figures from Ukraine’s railway operator cited by media outlets, attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.

Recent months have seen repeated attacks across the country on civilian infrastructure critical to daily life, including bridges, hospitals, schools, shopping centres and railway stations, Mr. Schmale said.
“The images from Dnipro cannot become another story that fades from attention. Behind every casualty is a person, a family and a future changed forever,” he said.
“It cannot be repeated often enough that civilians and civilian infrastructure are protected under international humanitarian law.”

Mr. Schmale told UN News in an interview on Thursday that preparations to get aid into Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Kherson region, were “accelerating” while a local ceasefire held, and that deliveries could arrive as early as Friday.
The ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump and announced by the White House on 23 October, is due to end on the evening of 1 November.
Ukraine’s Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has said he is on his way to the town and will accompany residents out.
Mr. Schmale said mined roads were a key reason residents had been trapped. He pointed to images of a stretch known locally as the “road of death”.
“It’s clear any safe passage both in and out has to have mine clearance preceding it,” he said, adding that reports reaching him confirmed demining was under way.
The UN has no direct role in the evacuation. “We have offered support, but it’s not been taken up,” Mr. Schmale said, adding that none of its partners were involved either.
Under established procedure, evacuees will get help once they reach Government-controlled areas.
That includes food and other material assistance, and possibly help finding housing. “There’s a high likelihood that we will get involved the minute they are here,” he said.
Mr. Schmale said estimates varied, but he had heard that 200 to 300 people might leave, “which would leave more than 1,000 there, and they would need support”.
He cited accounts from UN human rights monitors, civil society groups and the Ukrainian authorities.

The town’s remaining health facility was “barely functional” and short of medicine, he said, and keeping warm through winter amid energy disruption would be a growing challenge. Safe water and public infrastructure were also pressing needs.
“Because they’ve been trapped in that place for so long under heavy bombardment, mental health issues should never be overlooked,” he said.

articles.title: Vienna Open: Carlos Alcaraz survives tiebreak scare against Nikoloz Basilashvili as Daniil Medvedev beats Cameron Norrie

paras.en: Alcaraz battles into Vienna Open quarter-finals

Carlos Alcaraz outlasted Nikoloz Basilashvili in a second-set tiebreak to book his place in the third round of the Vienna Open; Daniil Medvedev was taken to a third set tiebreak by Cameron Norrie; watch live the Vienna Open live on Sky Sports

Carlos Alcaraz was forced to work hard to reach the quarter-finals of the Vienna Open, as the world No 3 was taken to a dramatic second-set tiebreak by Nikoloz Basilashvili, before he sealed a 6-1 7-6 (13-11) victory.
The Spaniard has now qualified for the 60th quarter-final in his ATP Tour career and will face Tommy Paul in the last eight.

Alcaraz raced to a commanding lead in the opening set, hitting nine winners before Basilashvili hit back in the second, responding to an early break from the Spaniard before saving two break points to force the tiebreak.
With Momentum on the Georgian's side, Basilashvili surged to a 4-1 lead in the tiebreak, but Alcaraz responded with a booming forehand to the baseline to draw level at 4-4.
The tension was high as they battled to 11-11, but despite his resilience, Basilashvili ultimately relented.
Daniil Medvedev vented his frustration on court as he sealed a 4-6 6-3 7-6(7-1) victory over Cameron Norrie at the Vienna Open.
Norrie and Medvedev traded sets before the Brit struck a brilliant cross-court winner to take a 3-0 lead in the decider.
Medvedev fumed, crouching on his left leg, before repeatedly punching the court with his fist.
He regrouped and staged an epic comeback to take the match to a tiebreak, in which Medvedev claimed seven points on the bounce to book a tie against French qualifier Adrian Mannarino.

articles.title: McCullum: Brook one of best tactical captains I've come across

paras.en: England head coach Brendon McCullum hails captain Harry Brook after tourists end ODI tri-series with consolation win

England boss Brendon McCullum talks Harry Brook's leadership, Adil Rashid's omission and the lessons learned as tourists earn victory at last in ODI tri-series; after missing out on the final, McCullum's men now focused on white-ball tour of Australia in November (three ODIs, five T20s)
Brendon McCullum called Harry Brook "one of the best tactical captains I've ever come across" after England ended a tough ODI tri-series with a consolation win over Sri Lanka in Lahore.

England lost their first three matches after a botched run chase against Pakistan was followed by failing to defend a total of 429 against Sri Lanka and then suffering another defeat to Pakistan as the hosts reached a target of 242 despite having been 154-9.

Brook's side looked in danger of a fourth loss from four when Pavan Rathnayake scored his second hundred against England in as many matches on Thursday but they eventually bowled Sri Lanka out for 331 as their opponents pursued a target of 387.
- England beat Sri Lanka as Ben Duckett, Liam Dawson star
- Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
- What cricket is live on Sky Sports and when? Full TV listings
Speaking to Sky Sports Cricket, head coach McCullum said of Brook: "He's one of the best tactical captains I've ever come across.
"He's got such an astute brain. He wears his intelligence lightly externally but he's a very switched on man and cricketer.
"He has the respect of the entire dressing room. He leads and they follow him. He is interactive with his leadership. It's not just him on his own, he calls on other people.
"He will have learned a lot from getting thrust into a situation like this where the game is travelling at breakneck speed, and you're having to make decisions which can win or lose a game.
"Providing you have the ability to take stock post-game, assess the situation and come up with new ideas [you can improve].
"We saw that [against Sri Lanka]. We were probably behind the game when they were five down but Brooky was able to slow it down, make some plays and we were able to get the wickets we needed.
"He would have grown enormously. I can't talk highly enough of his captaincy, not just his tactics but also his leadership."
Left-arm spinner Liam Dawson picked up the key wicket of Rathnayake, caught sweeping to short fine leg, in the 45th over with Sri Lanka needing 58 runs from 35 balls.

The 36-year-old bagged figures of 4-49 on the day and claimed seven wickets in three games at an average of 21.42 in the competition after replacing leg-spinner Adil Rashid following England's opening defeat to Pakistan in Rawalpindi.

Rashid, 38, is England's second-highest ODI wicket-taker of all time, behind only James Anderson, and McCullum suggested the Yorkshireman dropping out of the side in the tri-series was solely down to conditions.
The New Zealander added: "We will always do what we think is right for the conditions and the opposition we are playing against
"Dawson has done well out here with left-am spin having a significant impact on this tournament whereas leg-spin hasn't had much of a role.
"We want to be a team that can adapt to different conditions, be malleable and have that flexibility.
"Dawson is a highly-competitive player who has put his hand up and on this occasion, the conditions probably went against Rash."
'We know we need to get better - but we will'
England's preparations for the 2027 50-over World Cup in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe next take them to Australia in November with three ODIs followed by five T20 internationals.

Batter Jacob Bethell and fast bowler Jofra Archer will return after missing the tri-series in Pakistan due to a knee injury and rest respectively, but wicketkeeper-batter Jos Buttler remains sidelined while he recovers from hamstring surgery.
Bethell had been opening the batting with Ben Duckett in ODIs prior to his knee issue in the home summer, although may now face a battle to regain his spot immediately.

Tom Banton has struck one hundred, and four fifties, in seven innings since taking Bethell's place, while Duckett closed out the tri-series with successive centuries, including a career-best 167 from 132 balls.
McCullum says selection dilemmas are "good problems" to have as he reflected on what England have gleaned from their trip to the subcontinent.
"For us to be exposed at times but succeed at others - we have seen lot of guys step up and perform and others have great lessons learned from this trip," the head coach added.
"It is going to hold us in good stead moving forward. We know we had some missed opportunities in this series but we did some really good stuff.
"We bounced back in our final game, holding our nerve [with the ball] when the dewy conditions were against us. That was satisfying but we know we have a lot to learn.

"We want to be a team that challenges seriously for that World Cup and we know we need to get better - but we will. This experience has been very good for us, albeit it has been disappointing in terms of not making the final."

articles.title: Protests erupt in Spain after train crash kills dozens
articles.author: Michael Fiorentino

paras.en: URDA, Spain — Spain began three days of mourning Thursday after at least 74 people were killed and dozens more were injured in the country’s deadliest train crash in decades. But anger is mounting about the alleged incompetence that allowed the accident to happen and protesters clashed with police overnight outside the country’s Transportation Ministry in Madrid.
Once considered one of the country’s crowning achievements, Spain’s high-speed rail network had not endured a deadly crash since it came into service over 30 years ago.
After the second train accident in less than a year, the tragedy has deepened the feeling among many that there is something broken in the Spanish transportation system.

The crash follows weeks of protests in connection to rising costs and a housing shortage, which have already triggered massive and sometimes deadly demonstrations across the country, and piled the pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

On Wednesday, four weeks before the country goes to the polls in a national election, Sanchez visited the site in the central province of Toledo, where a quiet stretch of rail lined by olive groves had been turned into a scene of devastation.

Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off. Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident, which happened after one train crashed into another that was stationary on the line.
Spain’s Transportation Ministry said Thursday that the number of deaths had risen to 74.

More than 800 military and police personnel, over 200 vehicles, three helicopters, a mobile command post, drones, mounted units and search dogs, were brought in to rescue survivors and recover bodies, Spain’s Interior Ministry said Thursday.
Regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said that human remains had been found during rescue efforts, which now involved crane operations, particularly on a carriage that remained overturned.
A judge in Toledo barred anyone not involved in emergency, security, healthcare or judicial work from the crash site with an exclusion zone of around a mile of the site.

Spain’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, of whom one was killed and at least seven injured. Authorities said 57 of those injured remained in the hospital.
Several Americans were hurt, according to the State Department, which did not provide further details.
Jacksonville, Florida, firefighter Josue Garcia-Otero was on board with seven of his family members.

“We got to safety first, then began treating other patients that were critically injured,” Garcia-Otero said in a news release issued by the Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department. “My wife is a nurse, and she was helping too.”

Pledging an investigation and improvements to prevent a similar tragedy in future, Sánchez said “it was clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail.”

The prime minister said it was “not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.” In January, 46 people died in the south of the country after one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of a train going the opposite way.
Both crashes involved trains operated by the state-owned Renfe company and the privately owned IRYO.

Spain’s transportation minister, Oscar Puente, said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center to resume operations after a security system had failed.

Puente, who is facing calls to resign, said the train engineers were not to blame. A security system had stopped working because of a computer malfunction, causing all trains on the line to stop at about 8:30 a.m. local time (5:30 a.m. ET).

Shortly afterward, he said, central command had told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, adding that never should have happened and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.

Riot police used tear gas outside the Transportation Ministry late Wednesday after far-right protesters gathered outside and pushed against a cordon set up by officers. Some threw flares and other objects as some chanted slogans against Puente and Sánchez.

Quite what effect the accident will have on Sánchez’s political ambitions remains unclear. The prime minister called a snap election next month after his Socialist party suffered several defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country’s housing crisis.

Sanchez’s minority government had put forward two decree laws aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market after nationwide protests erupted following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid apartment. Maricarmen Abascal, who was in a wheelchair, was eventually allowed to return but died in the hospital before she could do so.
Sánchez, who took office in 2018, has weathered several crises during his premiership, including the Covid pandemic and the global inflation rise.

But he has faced attacks from right-wing parties over his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both deny. Polls show he is facing and uphill battle to win votes ahead of the election next month.

articles.title: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly fire that tested Beijing’s grip on city
articles.author: Mithil Aggarwal

paras.en: HONG KONG — Hong Kong’s leader made a rare apology Thursday for a residential fire that killed 168 people last year, announcing that a top housing official would resign after an investigation blamed corruption and regulatory failures for the Chinese territory’s worst human-caused disaster in decades.

The Nov. 26, 2025, fire at Wang Fuk Court, a high-rise housing estate in the suburban district of Tai Po, swiftly engulfed seven of its eight towers, killing 110 women and 58 men ranging in age from 6 months to 98 years old. Thousands of others were displaced from their homes at the complex, which was undergoing major renovations at the time of the blaze.

The tragedy provoked widespread public grief and anger and was widely seen as the first major test for the Hong Kong government since Beijing imposed a sweeping national security law in 2020 in response to pro-democracy protests. Critics say the law, which Hong Kong and Chinese officials say was necessary to restore stability, has been used to stifle dissent in the former British colony.

Calls for accountability and transparency after the fire were quickly met with warnings from Hong Kong and Chinese officials, who said that “external hostile forces” were trying to re-create the chaos of the 2019 protests, which sometimes turned violent.
John Lee, Hong Kong’s top leader, said he was “deeply saddened” by the fire’s impact on the community.
“After self-reflection, I have considered that the government should roll out a large number of measures for reform, and a lot of work has to be carried out,” he said at a news conference.
“In my capacity as chief executive, I apologize to all the victims and members of the public,” said Lee, who bowed in apology with seven other senior Hong Kong officials.

Lee said Housing Secretary Winnie Ho had resigned on Wednesday, making her the first official to lose her job over the fire. Ho “should bear political responsibility” for the disaster, he said, despite no evidence of personal wrongdoing.

Lee also said the government would make changes to Hong Kong’s construction industry and regulatory system based on recommendations from a scathing report by a government-appointed independent committee that was also released Thursday.

The fire was the result of “decades of failure by the bodies in positions of responsibility in the construction, fire safety engineering and building management industries, and the Government,” according to the 1,154-page report, which was submitted to the government last week and was partially redacted upon its public release.

The long-awaited report found that the fire was most likely caused by a lit cigarette that ignited combustible materials nearby. During public hearings earlier this year, the committee heard testimony that construction workers had been smoking on site.

Renovation contractors also used non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets and flammable foam boards to cover windows, which put the “lives of all residents in WF Court at serious risk, apparently with a view to maximizing their financial gains,” the report said.
The report said that Prestige Construction & Engineering Co., the main contractor, and project consultant Will Power Architects Co. had “cut corners in numerous aspects.”
“There is no doubt that they are the main culprits responsible for the occurrence of the inferno and the high fatalities in the tragic incident,” it said.
Both companies, along with seven individuals, were criminally charged in June on 25 counts, including manslaughter, money laundering and tax evasion.

The report also took a broader view of Hong Kong’s building maintenance and renovation sector, citing a “corrupt eco-system” long characterized by practices such as bid-rigging, which it recommended be criminalized.
In addition, the report criticized the government over regulatory lapses and a “slack enforcement attitude” at the housing complex, where residents had repeatedly raised safety concerns.
“The Committee finds that no Government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues, and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum,” the report said.

Lee said Thursday that the Housing Bureau, Buildings Department, Fire Services Department and Labor Department all bore some responsibility for the blaze and that all four agencies would be the subject of a three-month investigation.
John Burns, a professor emeritus of politics and public administration at the University of Hong Kong, said it was “very significant” that Lee had apologized.
“We’ve gone for years with no chief executive talking about political accountability, as though it didn’t exist,” he told NBC News in an interview.
“Today, we have the chief executive talking about this directly and talking about a system of political accountability,” Burns said. “That’s a positive step.”
He added that it was “inevitable” that an official such as Ho would resign, “otherwise the credibility of the government itself would have been even more severely damaged.”
